whoIsThisFor.heading: Who is the Tableau Consultant exam for?

personas.label: Analytics consultants
personas.description: You deliver Tableau projects for clients and want the credential that names the role.

personas.label: BI implementation leads
personas.description: You run the rollout: data sources, dashboards, publishing and getting people to use them.

personas.label: Solution architects
personas.description: You decide how Tableau fits with the rest of a client's data estate.

examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Consultant Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam is about delivering Tableau to an organisation, not just building views. It covers gathering requirements, preparing data, designing dashboards people will actually use, and publishing and governing them on Tableau Cloud or Server.
bullets: 63% to pass, about 38 correct answers out of 60. Confirm it in the official exam guide before you book.
Delivery, not just desktop. Expect discovery, data preparation, publishing, permissions and adoption.
Judgement questions. Several options will work; the right one fits the client's constraints.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: You are ready when you can take a vague business request, turn it into a data source and a dashboard, publish it with sensible permissions, and explain the choices. Aim for 75% or more on practice tests.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Consultant Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: You can take the exam online with a proctor or at a test centre. Here is what to expect:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Most questions describe a client situation, such as a dashboard nobody uses or a data source that is slow for everyone, and ask what the consultant should do.
bestWayToPass: Start from the question the business is asking: The right chart and the right data model both follow from it.
Know Tableau Prep: When to clean and shape data before it reaches the workbook, rather than with calculations inside it.
Learn published data sources: One governed source reused across workbooks is usually the answer to duplication and inconsistency.
Think about adoption: Training, subscriptions and alerts matter as much as the dashboard itself.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers delivering Tableau for an organisation: gathering requirements, preparing and publishing data, designing dashboards that get used, and managing permissions and adoption on Tableau Cloud or Server.

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Consultant: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: Discovery and Solution Design
blocks.body: A consultant's first job is to find the real question. Ask who the audience is, what decision the dashboard supports, how current the data must be, and what people do today instead. Those answers determine almost everything: a dashboard for executives wants a few clear numbers, while one for analysts wants filters and detail. Agree the measures and their definitions in writing, because disagreement about what revenue means causes more rework than any technical problem. Then decide where logic belongs: in the source system, in Tableau Prep, in a published data source, or in the workbook.

blocks.heading: Preparing Data with Tableau Prep
blocks.body: **Tableau Prep Builder** cleans and reshapes data before it reaches a workbook. Its steps include **clean** (rename, split, filter, change types), **join** and **union**, **aggregate**, **pivot** (turning columns into rows, which is how you fix spreadsheet-shaped data), and **output** to an extract or a published source. Doing this work in Prep rather than in workbook calculations means it happens once and every workbook benefits. Prep flows can be scheduled to run on a timetable so the output stays current.

blocks.heading: Published Data Sources and Governance
blocks.body: A **published data source** lives on Tableau Cloud or Server and can be reused by many workbooks. It carries its own joins, calculations, field names, descriptions and permissions. This is the main tool against the usual problem of five workbooks that each calculate revenue slightly differently. **Certification** marks a source as trusted so users can tell it apart from ad-hoc ones. Decide refresh schedules by how fresh the data must be, and remember that an extract refresh takes load off the source database while a live connection does not.

blocks.heading: Dashboard Design That Gets Used
blocks.body: Design for the audience and the device. Lead with the headline number, then the breakdown, then the detail. Use **actions** so a selection in one view filters or highlights another, and keep the number of filters on screen small, since each one costs performance and attention. Size the dashboard for how people will actually view it rather than for your own monitor. Use colour deliberately: one highlight colour draws the eye where you want it, while a rainbow of categories tells the reader nothing. Avoid putting everything on one dashboard; two focused dashboards beat one crowded one.

blocks.heading: Publishing, Permissions and Adoption
blocks.body: Content on Tableau Cloud or Server lives in **projects**, and permissions are best managed by **group** at the project level rather than per user per workbook. Plan who may view, who may edit and who may publish. **Subscriptions** email a view on a schedule and **data-driven alerts** notify people when a measure crosses a threshold, both of which bring users back without training them to remember. For adoption, launch with a small group, watch usage, and fix the first complaints quickly. A technically perfect dashboard nobody opens has not delivered anything.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Consultant Exam
scenarioTips.intro: Most questions give you a client problem and several workable answers. Pick the one that fits the audience, the data and the constraints described.

blocks.heading: Discovery
blocks.body: Who is the audience, what decision does this support, how fresh must the data be, and what do they do today? Everything else follows.

blocks.heading: Where Logic Belongs
blocks.body: Source system first, then Tableau Prep, then a published data source, then the workbook. The earlier it sits, the more reuse you get.

blocks.heading: Published Data Sources
blocks.body: One governed, certified source stops five workbooks disagreeing about the same measure.

blocks.heading: Dashboard Design
blocks.body: Headline, breakdown, detail. Few filters, deliberate colour, sized for the device people actually use.

blocks.heading: Adoption
blocks.body: Subscriptions and alerts bring users back. Launch small, watch usage, fix the first complaints fast.

sampleQuestions.question: Five workbooks each calculate revenue slightly differently and the numbers do not agree in meetings. What should the consultant recommend?
options: A training session on writing calculations
A certified published data source with the agreed calculation, reused by all workbooks
Switching all connections from extract to live
Rebuilding the five workbooks separately
sampleQuestions.explanation: One governed source with the agreed definition is what stops workbooks disagreeing, and certification signals it is the trusted one.
whyWrong: Training does not stop five separate definitions drifting apart again.
Connection type does not change how revenue is defined.
Rebuilding separately recreates the same problem.

sampleQuestions.question: A client's source data has monthly figures spread across twelve columns, one per month. What is the cleanest fix?
options: Write twelve calculated fields in the workbook
Create twelve separate data sources
Ask the client to retype the data
Pivot the columns into rows in Tableau Prep
sampleQuestions.explanation: Pivoting turns spreadsheet-shaped columns into rows, which is the shape Tableau works with, and doing it in Prep means every workbook benefits.
whyWrong: Twelve calculations repeat the problem in every workbook.
Twelve sources multiply the maintenance.
Retyping is error-prone and does not scale.

sampleQuestions.question: An executive dashboard is slow and cluttered, with fifteen filters on screen. What should the consultant do first?
options: Move it to a larger server
Cut it back to the few measures the executives actually decide on
Add more filters so users can narrow further
Switch every chart to a table
sampleQuestions.explanation: Executive audiences need a small number of clear numbers. Reducing scope fixes both the clutter and much of the slowness.
whyWrong: Hardware hides a design problem rather than fixing it.
More filters worsen both problems.
Tables are usually harder to read at a glance than charts.

sampleQuestions.question: A client needs the sales team notified when any region's weekly revenue falls below target. What fits?
options: A weekly meeting to review the dashboard
A subscription emailing the dashboard daily
A note in the dashboard title
A data-driven alert on that measure
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data-driven alerts fire when a measure crosses a threshold, which is exactly the requirement.
whyWrong: A meeting is slower and depends on someone noticing.
A daily email arrives whether or not anything is wrong.
A static note cannot react to data.

sampleQuestions.question: Where should permissions normally be managed on Tableau Cloud or Server?
options: By exporting dashboards as PDFs instead
Per user on each individual workbook
By group at the project level
By sharing passwords for a shared account
sampleQuestions.explanation: Group permissions set on projects scale and stay manageable as content and staff change.
whyWrong: PDFs lose interactivity and go stale immediately.
Per-user, per-workbook permissions become unmanageable quickly.
Shared accounts destroy accountability and security.

sampleQuestions.question: The business says it needs data 'in real time', but the source is a nightly warehouse load. What should the consultant do?
options: Build the dashboard on a manual spreadsheet upload
Refresh the extract every five minutes
Clarify how fresh the data genuinely needs to be
Switch to a live connection and promise real time
sampleQuestions.explanation: If the source only updates nightly, no Tableau setting makes it fresher. The requirement needs clarifying against what the data can support.
whyWrong: Manual uploads are less current and error-prone.
Frequent refreshes of unchanged data waste resources.
A live connection to a nightly warehouse still shows nightly data.

sampleQuestions.question: A dashboard will mostly be viewed on tablets in the field. What should the consultant account for?
options: Design and size the dashboard for that device
Increase the number of worksheets
Use a fixed 4K layout
Assume desktop sizing will adapt automatically
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dashboards should be designed for the device people actually use, since a desktop layout often becomes unusable on a smaller screen.
whyWrong: More worksheets makes the small-screen problem worse.
A 4K layout is unusable on a tablet.
Automatic resizing rarely produces a good small-screen layout.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main benefit of doing data cleaning in Tableau Prep rather than in workbook calculations?
options: It removes the need for permissions
The work happens once and every workbook using the output benefits
It makes the workbook file larger
It converts live connections to extracts automatically
sampleQuestions.explanation: Preparing data upstream means the logic is defined once, rather than repeated and varied in each workbook.
whyWrong: Permissions are still required on published content.
File size is not the point, and Prep output is usually smaller.
Connection type is a separate decision.

sampleQuestions.question: Six months after launch, usage data shows almost nobody opens the dashboard. What should the consultant investigate first?
options: Whether it answers a question the audience actually has
Whether to add more charts
Whether the colours match the brand
Whether to buy more licences
sampleQuestions.explanation: Low usage usually means the dashboard does not support a decision people are making, which is a discovery failure rather than a design detail.
whyWrong: Adding content to an unused dashboard does not create demand.
Branding rarely determines whether people use a dashboard.
More licences do not create usage.

sampleQuestions.question: A client wants one dashboard covering executive summary, regional detail and individual rep performance. What is the better approach?
options: Three copies of the same dashboard with different filters saved
One dashboard with every chart on it
Separate focused dashboards, linked, for each audience
A single giant crosstab
sampleQuestions.explanation: Different audiences need different views. Focused dashboards are faster, clearer and easier to maintain.
whyWrong: Three near-identical copies triple the maintenance.
One dashboard for three audiences serves none of them well.
A giant crosstab is slow and hard to read.

sampleQuestions.question: What does certifying a published data source communicate?
options: That it refreshes faster than other sources
That it is encrypted
That only administrators can use it
That it is a trusted, governed source users should prefer
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certification marks a source as reviewed and trusted, helping users choose it over ad-hoc alternatives.
whyWrong: Certification does not change refresh performance.
It is a trust marker, not an encryption setting.
Certified sources are meant to be widely used.

sampleQuestions.question: Stakeholders disagree about what counts as an active customer. What should the consultant do before building?
options: Build one version and let them react
Get the definition agreed and written down
Show both definitions on the same chart
Use the definition the most senior person prefers
sampleQuestions.explanation: Undocumented measure definitions cause rework and arguments later. Agreeing them first is cheaper than rebuilding.
whyWrong: Building first wastes effort when the definition changes.
Two competing numbers on one chart confuses the audience.
Seniority does not settle a definitional question correctly.

sampleQuestions.question: A published extract takes two hours to refresh and finishes after the morning meeting. What is a reasonable first step?
options: Reduce the extract: filter rows, drop unused fields, aggregate where possible
Switch everyone to a live connection
Move the meeting
Refresh twice as often
sampleQuestions.explanation: Smaller extracts refresh faster. Filtering, removing unused fields and aggregating are the standard levers.
whyWrong: A live connection may be slower still and loads the source database.
Changing the business to suit the tool is a last resort.
More frequent refreshes of a slow extract makes it worse.

sampleQuestions.question: Which sequence best reflects where calculation logic should live, most preferred first?
options: Workbook, published data source, Tableau Prep, source system
Wherever the developer prefers
Source system, Tableau Prep, published data source, workbook
Workbook only, always
sampleQuestions.explanation: The earlier logic sits, the more consumers reuse it and the less it drifts between workbooks.
whyWrong: That reverses the preference and maximises duplication.
Consistency matters more than individual preference.
Workbook-only logic cannot be reused.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the purpose of a subscription in Tableau Cloud or Server?
options: To email a view to users on a schedule
To certify a data source
To refresh an extract
To grant permission to edit a workbook
sampleQuestions.explanation: Subscriptions deliver a view by email on a timetable, which keeps users engaged without them remembering to look.
whyWrong: Certification is a trust marker on a data source.
Refresh schedules are configured separately.
Editing rights come from permissions.
